summary: Defines conceptual state machines for PANA, the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access, for both the client and the authentication agent. They show how PANA can interface with other components. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a board game, each side moves between steps by clear rules. This chart shows every step the two sides can be in and how they move.

questions: protocol for carrying authentication for network access
subtitle: State machine specifications for PANA client and authentication agent protocol implementations.

tldr.problem: PANA [RFC5191] uses EAP for authentication over network access, but implementations need a concrete specification of how the protocol progresses through states, what events trigger transitions, and how PANA coordinates with the EAP layer.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines two state machines: one for the PANA Client (PaC) and one for the PANA Authentication Agent (PAA). Each state machine specifies states, transition conditions, and actions. The machines show how PANA interfaces with EAP state machines to coordinate authentication messages and results.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have a clear model for how PANA protocol execution should behave, though implementations may use different internal methods while achieving the same results.

today: RFC 5609 is an Informational document that provides implementation guidance for [RFC5191]. It has not been obsoleted and remains the authoritative specification for PANA state machines.

sections.title: PANA Protocol and State Machine Concept
sections.content:
PANA (Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access) [RFC5191] transports authentication messages between two parties attempting to gain network access. A PANA protocol execution consists of message exchanges carrying EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) PDUs between a PaC (PANA Client) and a PAA (PANA Authentication Agent).

This document defines the conceptual state machines for both the PaC and PAA. A state machine models protocol execution as a sequence of states, with transitions triggered by events and conditions. Each transition executes actions (sending messages, starting timers, etc.) and moves to a new state. The state machines presented here are informative only—implementations may achieve identical results using different internal methods.

The PaC and PAA state machines are coordinated with EAP state machines defined in [RFC4137]. PANA acts as a lower layer for EAP, so the state machines show how PANA delivers EAP messages and receives EAP authentication results.
sections.plainLanguage: PANA is a set of rules for how two computers ask and answer questions to prove who they are. This shows all the steps each side goes through and what makes them move to the next step.

sections.title: PANA and EAP Layering
sections.content:
PANA carries EAP messages between an EAP Peer and an EAP Authenticator across a network. The architecture has two sides:

  • The PaC side has a PANA Client (PaC) state machine that interacts with an EAP Peer state machine to run PANA on behalf of the client.
  • The PAA side has a PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) state machine that interacts with an EAP Authenticator state machine to run PANA on behalf of the server.

The PaC and PAA state machines are responsible for actually transmitting and receiving PANA messages over the network. The EAP state machines handle the cryptographic authentication logic. PANA presents EAP messages to its peer EAP state machine, the EAP machine processes them, and returns results back through the PANA state machine.

Two interfaces are required: one between the PaC state machine and the EAP peer, and another between the PAA state machine and the EAP authenticator. These interfaces define how messages and authentication results are exchanged between layers.
sections.plainLanguage: PANA is the messenger that carries notes back and forth. EAP is the side that checks if the answers are correct. Both sides have a messenger and an answer-checker working together.

sections.title: PaC State Machine States and Transitions
sections.content:
The PANA Client state machine progresses through several states during a session:

  • INITIAL: The starting state. The PaC waits for either an authentication request from the application or a PAA-initiated handshake from the network.
  • WAIT_PAA: Awaiting response from the PAA. The PaC has sent a PANA-Auth-Answer and is waiting for the next PANA-Auth-Request with EAP data.
  • WAIT_EAP_MSG: Awaiting an EAP message from the EAP Peer state machine. The PaC holds the EAP response and waits for the Peer to generate a reply.
  • WAIT_EAP_RESULT: Awaiting the final EAP authentication result (success or failure) from the EAP Peer.
  • OPEN: The session is authenticated and established. The PaC can initiate re-authentication, liveness tests (pings), or session termination.
  • CLOSED: The session has ended. The PaC discards all state.

Transitions are triggered by events such as receiving PANA messages, EAP success/failure, timeouts, or application requests. Each transition may send PANA messages, start/stop timers, or call procedures like Authorize() or Disconnect().
sections.plainLanguage: The client starts waiting, then sends answers, then waits for results, then either opens the connection or closes it. While open, it can test if the connection is still working or ask to prove itself again.

sections.title: PAA State Machine States and Transitions
sections.content:
The PANA Authentication Agent state machine mirrors the client's logic from the server side:

  • INITIAL: The starting state. The PAA can begin authentication by sending an EAP request to the PaC, or wait for the PaC to initiate.
  • WAIT_PaC: The PAA has sent an EAP request and awaits the PaC's response message containing an EAP answer.
  • WAIT_EAP_RESULT: The PAA has passed the EAP response to its authenticator and awaits the final EAP success/failure result.
  • OPEN: The session is authenticated. The PAA can respond to re-authentication requests, liveness tests, or session termination initiated by the PaC.
  • CLOSED: The session has ended and all state is discarded.

Like the PaC, the PAA state machine interacts with its EAP state machine through defined interfaces. The PAA must authorize the client before transitioning to OPEN and must disconnect if authentication fails. Common procedures like retransmission, timeout handling, and session lifetime management apply to both machines.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks questions, waits for answers, checks them against its records, then either grants access or denies it. Once access is granted, it can respond to requests to re-prove identity or close the session.

sections.title: Message Exchange and Protocol Flow
sections.content:
PANA defines several message types with specific purposes:

  • PCI (PANA-Client-Initiation): The client starts authentication.
  • PAR/PAN: PANA-Auth-Request (from PAA) and PANA-Auth-Answer (from PaC) exchange EAP messages.
  • PTR/PTA: PANA-Terminate-Request and PANA-Terminate-Answer close the session.
  • PNR/PNA: PANA-Notification-Request and PANA-Notification-Answer for liveness tests (pings) and re-authentication.

Each message can carry flags (C for Complete, S for Start, A for Auth, P for Ping) that signal important state changes. The PaC and PAA coordinate timing using retransmission timers: if a message is not acknowledged within a timeout, it is retransmitted up to a maximum count. If the maximum is reached, the session times out and closes.

The state machines ensure reliable delivery by tracking which messages are outstanding and applying exponential backoff or fixed retransmission intervals. Session timeout is enforced to prevent indefinite open sessions, and an EAP response timeout limits how long the EAP layer is given to respond.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange labeled letters back and forth. If a letter does not get answered quickly enough, it is sent again. If too many tries fail, they give up and close the session.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations and Common Rules
sections.content:
The state machines define common procedures used in both PaC and PAA:

  • Authorize(): Creates or modifies authorization state. For the PaC it always succeeds; for the PAA it may fail if the EAP method does not generate keys or other requirements are not met.
  • key_available(): Checks whether a PANA authentication key exists, attempting to retrieve a Master Session Key (MSK) from the EAP layer if not.
  • Retransmission: Messages are cached and retransmitted if no acknowledgment arrives. The PaC and PAA cache the last sent answer so duplicates can be handled without reprocessing.
  • Session lifetime: A session timer expires based on Session-Lifetime AVP values or configured defaults, triggering SESS_TIMEOUT.

The state machines assume that nodes implement their own variation of these procedures. The document provides the conceptual model, but the actual internal implementation—message queuing, threading, asynchronous event handling—remains implementation-specific. Both PaC and PAA must reliably deliver messages and properly manage timers to ensure robust protocol behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides follow the same general rules: test that keys exist, resend messages that seem lost, and close sessions that have been open too long. How they do this inside their code is up to them.
